sentence: Metformin is a medicine that is used to treat type 2 diabetes.
note: NHS search summary: metformin can be used to treat type 2 diabetes.

sentence: The NHS says it can also be used for gestational diabetes and for a hormone condition it calls polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, or PMOS.
note: Summary lists gestational diabetes and PMOS; the existing entry calls this condition polycystic ovary syndrome, so the wording differs (flag for reviewer).

sentence: It is also used to help prevent type 2 diabetes in people at high risk of developing it.
note: Summary: also used to help prevent type 2 diabetes if at high risk.

sentence: Gestational diabetes is diabetes that first appears during pregnancy.
note: Plain definition, not in the retrieved text.

sentence: The NHS says metformin lowers blood sugar levels by improving the way the body handles insulin.
note: One NHS page described as lowering blood sugar by improving how the body handles insulin.

sentence: Another NHS description says it reduces the amount of sugar released by the liver and makes the body more sensitive to insulin.
note: Summary attributes this to another NHS page; exact page not stated, so both NHS metformin pages cited.

sentence: Metformin is usually taken as tablets, and there is a slow-release type.
note: NHS side-effects summary mentions standard tablets and slow-release tablets.

sentence: The NHS says the amount is increased slowly when standard tablets are first started, which lowers the chance of side effects.
note: Side-effects summary: advised to increase slowly, which reduces the chance of side effects.

sentence: The NHS lists feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, tummy pain and loss of appetite among the common side effects.
note: Both summaries list these as common.

sentence: A change in taste is also listed.
note: Side-effects summary lists changes in taste.

sentence: The NHS says most of these ease within a few weeks.
note: Summaries: ease after a couple of weeks / within a few weeks.

sentence: Taking metformin with a meal can help, and a doctor may suggest slow-release tablets if side effects are too much.
note: Summaries: take with a meal; doctor may suggest slow-release tablets.

sentence: Taking metformin for a long time can lower vitamin B12 levels, which can cause tiredness.
note: Summaries: vitamin B12 deficiency with long use; tiredness.

sentence: The NHS says a doctor can check levels, and if they become too low, vitamin B12 supplements will help.
note: Search 1 summary; attributed to NHS but exact page not stated.

sentence: Lactic acidosis, a build-up of acid in the blood, is a rare but serious side effect.
note: Summaries: lactic acidosis (too much acid in the blood) is rare and serious.

sentence: Symptoms the NHS lists include being sick, stomach pain, muscle cramps, breathing problems and severe tiredness.
The NHS says to call 999 if lactic acidosis or a severe allergic reaction is suspected.
note: Both summaries: call 999 for suspected lactic acidosis or anaphylaxis.

sentence: For other serious side effects, such as inflammation of the liver, the NHS says to call NHS 111.
note: Summary lists hepatitis as serious and says call NHS 111 for other serious side effects.

sentence: UK leaflets describe lactic acidosis as a medical emergency that needs hospital treatment.
note: Leaflet search: medical emergency, treated in hospital.

sentence: The NHS advises limiting how much alcohol is drunk while taking metformin, because it can increase the risk of serious side effects.
UK leaflets say drinking too much alcohol may increase the risk of lactic acidosis.
note: Leaflet search: avoid excessive alcohol since it may increase lactic acidosis risk.

sentence: The NHS asks people to tell the doctor before an X-ray or scan that uses iodine-based dye, or before surgery under general anaesthetic.
A review of manufacturer labels found that all of them advise stopping metformin before scans that use contrast dye.
note: Review summary; none specified how long.

sentence: UK leaflets say metformin may need to be paused for a short time during illness that causes fluid loss, such as vomiting, diarrhoea or fever.
One source says metformin is stopped temporarily if someone is dehydrated, and that the GP should be contacted.
The NHS says to call NHS 111 if more than the prescribed amount has been taken.
The NHS says most adults can take metformin, but some people should tell the doctor first.
These include people with uncontrolled diabetes, liver or kidney problems, a severe infection, heart failure or a high alcohol intake.
A past allergic reaction to metformin is also on the NHS list.
The risk of lactic acidosis is higher when the kidneys do not work well.
note: Summaries and leaflets say kidney problems raise the risk.

sentence: The NHS says metformin on its own will not usually affect the ability to drive, ride a bike or use machinery.
If dizziness occurs after taking it, the NHS says to wait until the dizziness stops before driving or using machinery.
One source says kidney function is checked before metformin is started and regularly after that.
note: Search 1 summary says before starting and at least yearly; yearly left out to avoid numbers; page not named.

sentence: The NHS says metformin can be taken in pregnancy, but advises checking with a doctor first.
A hospital leaflet says it can be used alone or together with insulin.
note: Pregnancy search; leaflet text blended with NHS pages.

sentence: The same source says that in gestational diabetes metformin is usually stopped after the birth.
For type 2 diabetes treated before pregnancy, the diabetes team advises on each case.
The NHS says that if the doctor or midwife says the baby is healthy, metformin can be taken while breastfeeding.
Only tiny amounts pass into breast milk, and no side effects have been linked with breastfed babies, the NHS says.
A review of manufacturer labels found they advise against metformin while breastfeeding, so labels and NHS advice differ.
The NHS says to call NHS 111 or speak to a health professional with any concern about the baby.
